blocks.text: A protocol is only as useful as the software actually built on top of it, and MCP now has a real, fast-growing world around it, official libraries to build with, servers other people have already written for you, and applications you can plug those servers straight into. This lesson is a tour of that landscape as it stands today, so you know what already exists before you consider building anything from scratch yourself.
1. The Open Specification and Reference SDKs

blocks.alt: An open specification provides a Python SDK and a TypeScript SDK

blocks.text: Everything in the ecosystem traces back to one open specification describing the message formats, the handshake, and the behavior of tools, resources, and prompts covered in earlier lessons. Alongside the specification, the protocol's creators publish reference SDKs, official libraries that implement the plumbing so individual developers do not need to hand-roll JSON-RPC framing themselves.

These SDKs are deliberately unopinionated about what your server or client actually does, they handle the protocol mechanics, initialize, discovery, message routing, and leave the interesting part, what your tools actually do, entirely up to you.
1.1 Where the Specification Lives

The specification is published openly, versioned by date, such as the 2025-06-18 version referenced in the MCP Workflow lesson, with a changelog describing exactly what changed between versions. Anyone building a server or client can check which protocol version they target and what capabilities that version defines.
2. The Python SDK

The official Python SDK is a common starting point for teams already working in a Python-heavy data or backend stack. It provides a small, decorator-based way of turning ordinary functions into MCP tools, handling schema generation from type hints automatically.
2.1 Installing and Running It

Once installed, the same script can run locally over stdio for testing during development, or be deployed behind a streaming HTTP transport for shared, remote use, without changing how the tools themselves are defined.
3. The TypeScript SDK

The official TypeScript SDK targets the Node.js ecosystem and is the natural fit for teams already building web backends or Electron-based desktop applications, several popular client hosts are themselves built on it. It exposes a similar tool-registration pattern, with schemas usually described using a validation library rather than hand-written JSON Schema.

Both official SDKs interoperate freely, a TypeScript host can talk to a Python server and vice versa, since neither side cares what language wrote the other, only that both speak the same JSON-RPC messages over the same transport.
3.1 Installing and Running It

The TypeScript SDK is a particularly common choice when the server needs to live alongside an existing Node.js backend, sharing types, validation logic, or database clients that backend already maintains.
4. Reference Servers Maintained by the Protocol Authors

blocks.alt: A file system server, GitHub server, and Slack server are reference servers

blocks.text: Beyond the SDKs, the protocol's creators also publish and maintain a small set of reference servers, working examples that double as genuinely useful tools, meant to demonstrate good practice and give the community a solid starting point to fork or extend.

blocks.text: 4.1 Why Reference Servers Matter Beyond Their Own Usefulness

Reference servers double as living documentation, a new developer learning to build their own server almost always starts by reading one of these, seeing firsthand how tool descriptions, schemas, and error handling look in working code rather than only in the abstract specification text.
5. The File System Server

The file system server is often the very first one people run, and for good reason, it is simple to understand and immediately useful, exposing tools like read_file, write_file, and list_directory scoped to one or more allowed root directories the user configures ahead of time. Scoping to specific directories is a deliberate safety boundary, not an oversight, an assistant should never be handed unrestricted access to an entire disk.
5.1 Typical Tools It Exposes

blocks.text: 6. The GitHub Server

A GitHub server typically exposes tools for reading and creating issues, opening pull requests, searching code, and inspecting commit history, turning natural-language requests like "open an issue for this bug" into an actual authenticated API call against a repository. Authentication is handled once, at server configuration time, using a personal access token or an installed app, the model itself never sees or handles credentials directly.
6.1 A Sample Tool Call Against It
7. The Slack Server

A Slack server commonly exposes tools to post messages, read recent channel history, or search across a workspace, letting an assistant summarize a busy channel or draft and send an update without a person copying text back and forth by hand. As with GitHub, workspace credentials live in the server's configuration, scoped to whatever permissions the workspace administrator has granted that integration.
7.1 A Sample Tool Call Against It
8. Database and Data Warehouse Servers

Community-built servers exist for popular databases, letting a model run read-only queries against a Postgres instance, browse a data warehouse's schema, or fetch rows matching a natural-language description translated into SQL. These servers usually enforce read-only access and row limits by default, a sensible precaution given that a model-generated query is not something you want running unrestricted writes against production data.

blocks.title: A recurring safety pattern
blocks.content: Nearly every widely used community server defaults to the narrowest reasonable permission, read-only where possible, a scoped directory instead of a whole disk, a single workspace instead of an entire organization. Loosening that default is an explicit choice the operator makes, not the starting point.

blocks.text: 8.1 Read-Only by Default, and Why

A model composing a SQL query from a natural-language request is not guaranteed to compose the query its author actually intended, a subtle misunderstanding could turn a report request into a query that touches far more rows than expected. Restricting the underlying database credentials to read-only access removes that entire class of risk regardless of what query gets generated.
9. Client Applications That Speak MCP Today

blocks.alt: A chat app and an IDE both speak MCP

blocks.text: On the other side of the ecosystem sit the host applications people actually open, desktop AI assistants with built-in MCP support, letting a user add a server through a simple configuration file or settings panel and immediately gain access to whatever tools that server exposes. These hosts handle the client-side plumbing entirely, a user never sees a JSON-RPC message, they just see new capabilities appear.
9.1 A Typical Configuration Entry

A configuration entry like this is usually the entire setup burden for a user, name a server, tell the host how to start it, and everything else, discovery, capability exchange, tool calls, happens automatically from that point on.
10. IDEs and Coding Assistants as Hosts

blocks.alt: An IDE acts as a host

blocks.text: Several AI-enabled code editors and coding assistants act as MCP hosts as well, connecting simultaneously to a file system server, a terminal or shell server, and a version control server, giving a coding assistant a consistent way to read a project, run commands, and inspect git history, all through the same protocol rather than three separate bespoke integrations.
10.1 Why Editors Adopted MCP Quickly

Coding assistants were already juggling several bespoke integrations, a terminal runner, a file reader, a git wrapper, each built and maintained separately before MCP existed. Consolidating those into MCP servers meant editor vendors could delete a pile of one-off integration code and let the community's servers cover the same ground, often better, since more people were testing and improving them.
11. How the Ecosystem Grows Through Open Contribution

blocks.alt: A contributor adds a new server, growing the ecosystem

blocks.text: Because the specification and the reference SDKs are open, anyone can write and publish a new server without asking permission from the protocol's maintainers, the same open-contribution pattern that let package ecosystems like a language's standard package registry grow far larger than any single company could have built alone.
A developer who needs a server for some internal tool their company uses can build one, and often chooses to publish it for anyone else facing the same need.

This is precisely the ecosystem effect predicted in the Why MCP lesson's discussion of shared servers and shared benefit, once a server for a popular tool exists and works well, every team that needed that same integration gets it for free instead of writing their own from scratch.
11.1 What Makes a Server Worth Publishing

items: It solves a real, recurring need, not just a one-off personal script.
Its tool descriptions and schemas are clear enough for a model to use correctly without extra hand-holding.
It defaults to the narrowest reasonable permissions rather than the broadest.
It is documented well enough that someone unfamiliar with the underlying system can still configure it.

blocks.text: 12. Registries and Directories for Discovering Servers

As the number of community servers grew, searchable directories and registries appeared, letting a developer look up whether a server already exists for the tool they need before writing one themselves, along with basic metadata, what it exposes, how actively it is maintained, and how to install it.

code.content:
# a rough sketch of what a registry entry captures
{
  "name": "slack-server",
  "maintainer": "community",
  "tools": ["post_message", "read_channel_history", "search_messages"],
  "install": "npx @some-scope/slack-mcp-server"
}

blocks.text: 12.1 What to Check Before Installing a Third-Party Server

items: Who maintains it, and how recently it was updated.
Exactly which tools and permissions it requests.
Whether its source code is available to read before you run it.
Whether other users have reported issues with it in the registry or its repository.

blocks.text: 13. Worked Example: Assembling an Ecosystem-Native Assistant

blocks.alt: A file server and GitHub server combine into an assembled assistant

blocks.text: Imagine a small engineering team wants an assistant that can read internal documentation files, open GitHub issues, and post updates to a Slack channel. Nobody on the team needs to write a single MCP server from scratch, they configure a host application to connect to three already-existing community servers, file system, GitHub, and Slack, each running independently, and the assistant immediately gains all three abilities.

items: File system server, scoped to the documentation folder only.
GitHub server, authenticated with a token scoped to one repository.
Slack server, authenticated with a token scoped to one workspace.

blocks.text: Building the equivalent by hand, three separate vendor-specific integrations, would have taken considerably longer than writing three lines of server configuration against tools the community had already built and tested.
14. Common Mistakes When Navigating the Ecosystem

items: Writing a brand new server for a tool that already has a well-maintained community server available.
Installing a community server without checking what permissions and credentials it actually requests first.
Assuming every server in a public registry is equally maintained or trustworthy, quality and update frequency vary a great deal.
Picking an SDK based on hype rather than which language the rest of the team's codebase already uses.
Forgetting that a host still needs to be configured to trust and connect to a new server, simply having it installed somewhere is not enough.

blocks.text: 15. Practice: Map Your Own Toolchain to the Ecosystem

List three tools or systems your own work depends on, an internal wiki, a ticketing system, a cloud provider's dashboard, whatever comes to mind. For each one, search for whether a community MCP server already exists for it, and note what you find.

code.content:
my_tools = ["internal wiki", "ticketing system", "cloud dashboard"]
# for each: does a community MCP server already exist? what does it expose?

blocks.text: For any tool without an existing server, sketch, in a sentence or two, what the two or three most useful tools such a server would need to expose.
Key Takeaway

MCP today is far more than a specification on paper, it is official SDKs in Python and TypeScript, a growing library of community-built servers for the tools teams already use, and client applications, from desktop assistants to coding editors, that let people plug those servers in without writing any protocol code themselves.

This lesson mapped what already exists, the next lesson, MCP vs Traditional Tool Calling, turns to comparison, setting MCP side by side with the hand-rolled, vendor-specific function calling patterns many teams were using before this ecosystem existed.
